name.text: 01 Content: Visual Identity Is Not Computational Identity

questiontext.text:
Visual Identity Is Not Computational Identity

Two strings of Greek appear on your screen. They are rendered by the same font at the same size, and they are pixel-for-pixel identical. A search for one does not find the other. Your XSLT transformation processes one and silently skips the other. Your collation software reports a variant where you can see no difference whatsoever.

This is not a malfunction. It is the single most important fact about digital Greek, and the whole of this lesson follows from it: what you see is not what is stored. The screen displays graphemes — units of writing — while the computer stores code points, numeric values standing for characters. The relationship between the two is not one-to-one, and for polytonic Greek it is emphatically not one-to-one.

The consequence for a digital edition is severe, because every operation that matters is performed on the stored bytes rather than on the rendered image. Searching, sorting, collation, morphological analysis, error-rate measurement, schema validation — all compare code point sequences. Two visually identical readings that differ in their underlying encoding are, to every tool in your pipeline, two different readings.

Boschetti (2010), working on the Homer Multitext and on improving OCR accuracy for classical critical editions, treats orthographic and encoding normalization as prerequisite to any analytical work rather than as cleanup afterwards. The ordering is deliberate: analysis performed on inconsistently encoded text produces results that are wrong in ways that do not announce themselves.

Vocabulary. Grapheme — the smallest unit of a writing system as a reader perceives it. Code point — a numeric value in the Unicode standard, written U+03B1. Rendering — the process by which a font turns code points into visible marks.

Takeaway: Identical appearance on screen does not imply identical storage, and every tool in your pipeline compares storage.

name.text: 02 Content: The Hellenistic Invention of the Diacritical System

questiontext.text:
The Hellenistic Invention of the Diacritical System

The complexity you are about to encode is not an artifact of computing. It originates in a scholarly intervention made more than two thousand years ago, for reasons that are recognizably philological.

Ancient Greek was originally written without accents, breathings, or word division — a continuous stream of capital letters known as scriptio continua. This was adequate while the language was spoken natively, because readers supplied pronunciation from competence. By the Hellenistic period that condition was failing: Attic Greek of the classical authors was diverging from the spoken Koine, the pitch accent was collapsing toward a stress accent, and readers at Alexandria could no longer reliably reconstruct the pronunciation of the texts they were preserving.

The response, associated with Aristophanes of Byzantium in the third and second centuries BCE, was a system of marks recording exactly the information that was being lost: the position and contour of the pitch accent, and the presence or absence of initial aspiration. The diacritics are, in origin, a preservation technology — an editorial apparatus for pronunciation, added by scholars to texts that were already old.

This history explains a fact you will confront directly in Week 6. Diacritics are editorial, not authorial. The manuscripts you will transcribe carry accentuation supplied by scribes centuries after composition, applied inconsistently, and sometimes wrongly. When you make normalization decisions about accents in Week 6, you are adjudicating between editorial traditions rather than recovering an author's intention — and the difference matters for how you justify the decision.

Takeaway: Greek diacritics are a Hellenistic editorial apparatus for recording pronunciation, not part of the original written text.

name.text: 03 Content: The Accents: Oxia, Varia, Perispomeni

questiontext.text:
The Accents: Oxia, Varia, Perispomeni

The polytonic system marks three accent contours, each originally denoting a distinct pitch movement on the accented syllable.

Accent Greek name Mark Original phonetic value Example
Acute oxia (ὀξεῖα) ´ Rising pitch λόγος
Grave varia (βαρεῖα) ` Suppressed or lowered pitch ἀγαθὸς λόγος
Circumflex perispomeni (περισπωμένη) ῀ Rising then falling on one syllable δῶρον

The grave is the one with an editorial dimension you should understand now. It is not an independent accent so much as a contextual variant: an acute on a final syllable is written as a grave when another word follows without intervening punctuation. The same word therefore appears with different accentuation depending on its position in the sentence.

This creates a genuine encoding problem rather than a merely orthographic one. If you are collating witnesses, is ἀγαθός in one manuscript and ἀγαθὸς in another a textual variant, or the same word in different syntactic environments? The answer depends on context, and the decision must be made explicitly and recorded — it cannot be delegated to software, which sees two different code point sequences and will report a difference.

The circumflex introduces a separate problem, this time typographic. It is represented in different traditions by a tilde-like mark or by an inverted breve, and different fonts render the same code point differently. The code point is unambiguous; the visual form is not. Judge encoding by inspecting code points, never by inspecting the rendered glyph.

Takeaway: Three accents encode pitch contour, and the grave is a positional variant of the acute — which makes it a collation decision, not an automatic one.

name.text: 04 Content: The Breathings: Dasia and Psili

questiontext.text:
The Breathings: Dasia and Psili

Every word-initial vowel in polytonic Greek carries a breathing mark, and initial rho carries one too. There are two.

The rough breathing (dasia, δασεῖα), written as a mark resembling an opening single quote, indicates initial aspiration — an /h/ sound preceding the vowel, as in ὁδός (hodos, "road"). The smooth breathing (psili, ψιλή), resembling a closing single quote, indicates the absence of aspiration, as in ὀδούς (odous, "tooth").

The smooth breathing is worth pausing on, because it is where students most often go wrong. It marks a negative: it asserts that there is no aspiration. A reader might reasonably expect the absence of a sound to be represented by the absence of a mark, but the system is explicit in both directions. A vowel-initial word with no breathing mark at all is not "unaspirated" — it is unmarked, which is a different claim, and in a diplomatic transcription it is a claim about the manuscript rather than about the language.

This distinction becomes an editorial decision in Week 4. Many manuscripts, particularly earlier ones and those in hands working quickly, omit breathings irregularly. A diplomatic transcription must record the omission faithfully; a normalized transcription supplies the missing mark. Recording which you have done — and being able to move between the two — is precisely what the <orig>/<reg> markup you meet in Week 6 exists to support (TEI Consortium, 2026).

Note also that breathings and accents co-occur on the same vowel constantly, and their combination is where the encoding problems of the next several pages originate: a single alpha may carry a breathing, an accent, and an iota subscript simultaneously.

Takeaway: Smooth breathing marks the positive absence of aspiration, so an unmarked vowel in a manuscript is a different fact from a smooth-breathed one.

name.text: 05 Content: Diaeresis, Iota Subscript, and Iota Adscript

questiontext.text:
Diaeresis, Iota Subscript, and Iota Adscript

Three further marks complete the polytonic inventory, and each carries an encoding consequence.

The diaeresis (¨) marks a vowel that is not part of a diphthong with the preceding vowel — a separation instruction, as in ἀΐδιος, where the iota is pronounced independently. Unlike accents and breathings it makes a claim about syllabification rather than about pitch or aspiration, and it can co-occur with an accent on the same vowel.

The iota subscript (ypogegrammeni, ῳ ῃ ᾳ) is the historical trace of a long diphthong whose iota ceased to be pronounced. Ancient manuscripts wrote the iota on the line, as a full letter — the iota adscript (ωι ηι αι). The subscript form is a Byzantine and later editorial convention, introduced to record a letter that was no longer sounded.

The distinction is directly consequential for your transcription. A manuscript may write the adscript, may write the subscript, or may omit the iota entirely, and these are three different states of the evidence:

Manuscript form Encoding Editorial status
Iota adscript (ωι) Two code points: omega + iota The older written practice; transcribe as written
Iota subscript (ῳ) One precomposed point, or omega + U+0345 Later convention; a normalization if supplied
Iota omitted (ω) Omega alone May be scribal error or may reflect pronunciation

Deciding how to handle this in your own edition is a Week 6 task, but you should be able to see the shape of the problem already: silently converting adscript to subscript is an editorial intervention, and one that a reader cannot detect unless you record it.

Vocabulary. Ypogegrammeni — the "written under" iota, U+0345. Adscript — the same historical iota written as a full letter on the line.

Takeaway: Iota subscript is a later editorial convention for an adscript the manuscripts wrote in full, so converting between them is an intervention that must be recorded.

name.text: 06 Content: Beta Code and the Legacy Encoding Era

questiontext.text:
Beta Code and the Legacy Encoding Era

Before Unicode, representing this system on computers required improvisation, and the improvisation that dominated classical scholarship was Beta Code.

Beta Code represents polytonic Greek using only the 7-bit ASCII character set — the 128 characters available on early terminals and mainframes. Each Greek letter maps to a Latin letter, and each diacritic to a punctuation mark, with the marks following the letter in a defined order. The word ἀγαθός is written *A)GAQO/S, in which ) is the smooth breathing, Q is theta, and / is the acute.

The scheme was ingenious and it worked. The Thesaurus Linguae Graecae was built on it, and an enormous quantity of digitized classical text still exists in Beta Code or in formats derived from it. You will very likely encounter it this term in older datasets.

Its cost, however, was structural rather than merely cosmetic. Beta Code represents a single Greek grapheme as a sequence of ASCII characters, which severs the graphemic unity of the character: to the computer, ἀ is not one thing with properties but three unrelated symbols in a row. Sorting, searching, and counting all operate on that sequence rather than on the letter, and every program must implement its own logic to reassemble graphemes from it.

Boschetti (2010) notes a related loss in early digital libraries, which prized breadth of coverage over depth of representation — digitizing the canonical texts while discarding the critical apparatus and paratextual material that make an edition scholarly. The two losses share a cause: an infrastructure that could not represent complexity encouraged projects to shed it.

Takeaway: Beta Code encoded Greek as ASCII sequences, severing the unity of the grapheme and forcing every program to reassemble letters for itself.

name.text: 07 Content: Unicode's Architecture for Greek

questiontext.text:
Unicode's Architecture for Greek

Unicode replaced the legacy schemes with a single universal character set in which Greek letters are Greek letters rather than repurposed Latin ones. For polytonic Greek, three blocks matter (Unicode Consortium, 2025).

Block Range Contains Primary use
Greek and Coptic U+0370–U+03FF Basic letters, monotonic accented forms Modern Greek; base letters for composition
Greek Extended U+1F00–U+1FFF Precomposed polytonic combinations Ancient Greek with accents and breathings
Combining Diacritical Marks U+0300–U+036F Accents and breathings as separate marks Building accented forms compositionally

The Greek and Coptic block supplies the alphabet: alpha is U+03B1, omega is U+03C9. These are the letters without polytonic diacritics, plus the accented forms that modern monotonic Greek requires.

The Greek Extended block exists specifically for ancient Greek. It contains precomposed characters — single code points standing for a base letter together with all its diacritics. Alpha with smooth breathing and acute is one code point, U+1F04. Alpha with smooth breathing, acute, and iota subscript is also one code point, U+1F84. There are several hundred such combinations, enumerated exhaustively.

The Combining Diacritical Marks block takes the opposite approach. Rather than enumerating combinations, it supplies the marks as independent code points that follow a base letter and modify it. Smooth breathing is U+0313, acute is U+0301, ypogegrammeni is U+0345. Any combination can be built by concatenation, including combinations for which no precomposed character exists (Unicode Consortium, 2025).

Takeaway: Unicode provides both precomposed polytonic characters in Greek Extended and composable marks in Combining Diacritical Marks — two routes to the same grapheme.

name.text: 08 Content: The Two Ways to Write One Letter

questiontext.text:
The Two Ways to Write One Letter

The existence of two routes is the source of the problem this lesson opened with. Take ἀ — alpha with smooth breathing. It can be encoded as:

Route Code points Length Where it typically originates
Precomposed U+1F00 1 character Windows input; Greek Extended keyboards
Decomposed U+03B1 U+0313 2 characters macOS input; some web forms and OCR output

Both render as ἀ. Any font that supports polytonic Greek displays them identically, and no visual inspection can distinguish them. But their stored representations differ in both length and content, and therefore:

  • A byte-level comparison evaluates them as unequal.
  • A character count returns 1 for one and 2 for the other.
  • A search for one does not match the other.
  • A regular expression matching a single character matches only the precomposed form.
  • An XSLT template matching on the string processes only one of them.

For a longer word the divergence compounds. ᾧ — omega with rough breathing, circumflex, and iota subscript — is one code point precomposed, and up to four decomposed. A twenty-line transcription may differ in hundreds of code points from a visually identical transcription of the same passage.

Unicode calls these two forms canonically equivalent: the standard asserts that they represent the same abstract character and that conforming software should treat them as the same (Unicode Consortium, 2025). The word "should" is doing heavy lifting. Software that compares strings byte by byte — which is most software, including Git, most search tools, and most XML processors — does not implement canonical equivalence, and will treat them as different.

Takeaway: Precomposed and decomposed forms are canonically equivalent by the standard but unequal to most software, which compares bytes.

name.text: 09 Content: The Four Normalization Forms

questiontext.text:
The Four Normalization Forms

Unicode's solution is normalization: transforming text into a defined canonical representation so that equivalent strings become identical strings. Unicode Standard Annex #15 defines four forms (Unicode Consortium, 2025).

Form Full name Operation Lossy?
NFD Normalization Form D Canonical decomposition: split every character into base plus marks No
NFC Normalization Form C Canonical decomposition, then canonical composition: prefer precomposed No
NFKD Normalization Form KD Compatibility decomposition: also collapses formatting distinctions Yes
NFKC Normalization Form KC Compatibility decomposition, then composition Yes

The distinction that matters is the canonical / compatibility split, not the composed / decomposed one. Canonical forms — NFC and NFD — preserve all information: converting between them is fully reversible, and no distinction the text made is lost. Compatibility forms — NFKC and NFKD — deliberately discard distinctions the standard regards as formatting rather than content.

The K forms are dangerous for philology, and it is worth being concrete about why. Compatibility decomposition maps superscript characters to ordinary ones, ligatures to their constituent letters, and various presentation variants to base forms. In a scholarly context those distinctions are frequently the data: a superscript abbreviation mark, a manuscript ligature, or a presentation form recorded from the source is content, and NFKC silently destroys it.

Never apply NFKC or NFKD to manuscript transcription. They are appropriate for search index construction, where collapsing distinctions is the point, and for nothing else in this course.

Takeaway: Use the canonical forms NFC and NFD, which are lossless; the compatibility forms NFKC and NFKD destroy distinctions that are philological data.

name.text: 10 Content: Why This Course Mandates NFC

questiontext.text:
Why This Course Mandates NFC

Between the two lossless forms, this course requires NFC — precomposed wherever a precomposed character exists. Three reasons, in order of weight.

First, interoperability. NFC is the form specified for text on the Web and the form assumed by the great majority of XML tooling, database collations, and text processing libraries. Producing NFC means your edition behaves correctly in software you did not write and cannot inspect, which describes nearly everything your files will eventually pass through.

Second, compactness and predictability of length. In NFC, ᾧ is a single character; in NFD it is up to four. Character offsets, line lengths, and the character error rates you will compute in Week 5 all depend on what counts as a character, and the NFC count corresponds to what a human reader would say if asked how many letters a word has.

Third, and most important for this course, comparability. Every measurement you perform in Week 5 compares a machine transcription against your manual ground truth. If the two are in different normalization forms, the comparison is meaningless — a character error rate computed across a normalization mismatch can report tens of percent error on two transcriptions that are in fact identical. You would then spend an afternoon correcting a model that was already correct.

The requirement is therefore not stylistic. Encode in NFC because in Week 5 you will subtract one transcription from another, and that subtraction is only valid if both are in the same form.

Takeaway: NFC is required because Week 5's error-rate comparison is only meaningful if ground truth and machine output are in the same normalization form.

name.text: 11 Content: Canonical Combining Class and the Ordering of Marks

questiontext.text:
Canonical Combining Class and the Ordering of Marks

One further mechanism is needed before normalization is well defined. When a letter carries several marks — breathing, accent, and iota subscript together — in what order are the combining code points stored? If the order were free, then two decomposed sequences could contain the same marks in different orders and still fail to compare equal, and normalization would not have solved the problem.

Unicode fixes the order using the Canonical Combining Class (CCC), a numeric property assigned to every code point, ranging from 0 to 254. Marks are sorted by CCC value during normalization, so a given set of marks always yields one sequence (Unicode Consortium, 2025).

Code point Mark CCC Effect on ordering
U+0301 Combining acute 230 Sorts among above-letter marks
U+0313 Combining comma above (psili) 230 Sorts among above-letter marks
U+0345 Combining ypogegrammeni 240 Sorts after above-letter marks

The ypogegrammeni's higher class places it consistently at the end of a combining sequence, which is why ᾆ decomposes to a fixed order rather than an arbitrary one (Unicode Consortium, 2025). Marks with class 0 are not reordered at all; marks sharing a class are left in their existing relative order, because for marks at the same position the order can be visually significant.

You will not manipulate CCC values by hand. It matters because it is the reason normalization is deterministic — the guarantee that normalizing the same abstract text always produces the same bytes, on any platform, in any implementation. That determinism is what lets you treat a normalized file's hash as a meaningful identity, which is exactly what Lesson 1.1's argument about content-addressable storage depends on.

Takeaway: Canonical Combining Class fixes the order of multiple marks, which is what makes normalization deterministic across platforms.

name.text: 12 Content: The macOS and Windows Divergence

questiontext.text:
The macOS and Windows Divergence

The abstract problem becomes a concrete classroom problem because operating systems differ in which form they produce by default.

macOS has historically normalized filenames to a variant of NFD at the file system level, and macOS input methods and text services tend to produce decomposed sequences. Windows favours precomposed NFC, and its Greek keyboard layouts emit precomposed characters from Greek Extended. Linux behaviour varies by input method and application, and cannot be assumed either way.

The result in a mixed-platform class is a failure mode that is genuinely invisible. Consider a peer review in Week 5. Your partner, on a Mac, transcribes a passage in NFD. You, on Windows, open the file and correct three words, and your editor writes your corrections in NFC. You commit. The diff shows changes on lines you never touched, because those lines were rewritten from NFD to NFC by your editor — or, worse, shows no changes on lines you did touch, because a whitespace-collapsing viewer hid the difference.

Now recall the previous lesson: Git compares bytes. It will faithfully report a difference it cannot explain, on lines whose rendered appearance is unchanged. Students confronted with this conclude that Git is broken. Git is working perfectly; the text is in two forms.

Worse still is the merge case. Two students edit the same line in different normalization forms. Git reports a conflict. Both students look at the conflict markers, see two identical-looking lines of Greek, and have no way to resolve it by inspection — the difference is real, structural, and invisible.

Takeaway: macOS tends to produce NFD and Windows NFC, so a mixed-platform team generates conflicts that are structurally real and visually undetectable.

name.text: 13 Content: Normalizing with Python's `unicodedata`

questiontext.text:
Normalizing with Python's `unicodedata`

The remedy is mechanical. Python's standard library includes unicodedata, whose normalize function implements all four forms (Python Software Foundation, n.d.).

import unicodedata

decomposed = "ἀ"          # alpha + combining psili
composed = unicodedata.normalize("NFC", decomposed)

print(decomposed == composed)        # False - different code points
print(len(decomposed), len(composed))  # 2 1
print(f"{ord(composed):04X}")        # 1F00

The function takes the target form as a string and returns the normalized text. It is available in every standard Python installation with no dependencies, which matters for a course in which everyone must be able to run the same script.

A practical script for a whole file:

import unicodedata
from pathlib import Path

def normalize_file(path: Path, form: str = "NFC") -> bool:
    """Rewrite path in the given normalization form. Return True if changed."""
    original = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    normalized = unicodedata.normalize(form, original)
    if original == normalized:
        return False
    path.write_text(normalized, encoding="utf-8")
    return True

Two details deserve attention. The function returns whether it changed anything, which lets a calling script report what it touched rather than rewriting files silently — you want to know when normalization was needed. And the encoding is declared explicitly on both read and write: relying on the platform default encoding is exactly the kind of implicit platform dependence this lesson is about.

Takeaway: unicodedata.normalize("NFC", text) is the whole mechanism, available in any standard Python installation.

name.text: 14 Content: Automating Normalization at Commit Time

questiontext.text:
Automating Normalization at Commit Time

Knowing the remedy is insufficient, because normalization must be applied every time and human memory does not work that way. Attach it to the pre-commit hook introduced in Lesson 1.1, so that no unnormalized text can enter the history.

#!/bin/sh
# .git/hooks/pre-commit
python3 tools/normalize_nfc.py --staged || exit 1

The script should operate on the staged files specifically, obtainable with git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=ACM. Having normalized a file, it must re-stage it with git add, or the commit will record the pre-normalization content while the working directory holds the normalized version — a discrepancy that is confusing to diagnose.

Step Command or call Purpose
List staged text files git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=ACM Restrict work to what is being committed
Normalize each unicodedata.normalize("NFC", text) Convert to the mandated form
Re-stage changed files git add <file> Ensure the commit records normalized bytes
Report print changed paths Make the intervention visible, not silent

Keep the script in a tracked tools/ directory and install it into .git/hooks/ with a setup script, for the reason given in Lesson 1.1: hooks are not cloned.

The pedagogical argument for automation is that it removes a burden without removing the understanding. You still need to know what NFC is, why it is required, and how to detect a violation — that knowledge is examinable and is what lets you diagnose the problem when it appears in someone else's files. What you do not need is to remember to run a command every time, because that is the part humans reliably fail at.

Takeaway: Enforce NFC in the pre-commit hook and re-stage the normalized file, so unnormalized text cannot enter the repository.

name.text: 15 Content: Verifying Encoding by Inspecting Code Points

questiontext.text:
Verifying Encoding by Inspecting Code Points

Because the problem is invisible on screen, you need a habit of looking beneath the rendering. Learn to dump code points.

import unicodedata

def inspect(text: str) -> None:
    for ch in text:
        print(f"U+{ord(ch):04X}  {unicodedata.name(ch, '<unnamed>')}")

inspect("ᾧ")

For a file already in NFC, the output names one character. For the same grapheme in NFD, it names a base letter followed by combining marks. This is the ground truth about your data, and it is the only reliable way to answer the question "what is actually in this file?"

Command-line equivalents are worth knowing, since you will often want to check a file without opening Python:

Task Command
Dump code points of a file python3 -c "import sys;[print(f'U+{ord(c):04X}') for c in sys.stdin.read()]" < file.xml
Check whether a file is already NFC python3 -c "import sys,unicodedata as u;t=sys.stdin.read();print(t==u.normalize('NFC',t))" < file.xml
Show bytes with offsets xxd file.xml
Count characters versus bytes wc -m file.xml and wc -c file.xml

The second command is the one to reach for when a diff looks wrong. If it prints False, the file is not normalized and that is very likely your explanation.

Build the habit now, on files you understand. In Week 5, when an error rate comes back implausibly high, the first hypothesis to test is a normalization mismatch, and you will want the check to be reflexive rather than something you have to work out under time pressure.

Takeaway: When Greek text behaves strangely, dump the code points — the rendering cannot tell you what is stored.

name.text: 16 Content: Fonts for Polytonic Greek

questiontext.text:
Fonts for Polytonic Greek

A font maps code points to glyphs. If a font lacks a glyph for a code point, the text is not wrong — it simply cannot be displayed, and you will see a replacement box. Students routinely mistake this for data corruption and "fix" correct files.

Not every Unicode font covers the Greek Extended block, and coverage of rare combinations is uneven even among fonts that advertise polytonic support. Choose a font with documented coverage and use it consistently.

Font Coverage Notes
Gentium Plus Full polytonic; extensive diacritics Free; designed for linguistic and philological use
New Athena Unicode Full polytonic, epigraphic and papyrological marks Free; standard in classics
Brill Full polytonic, extensive scholarly range Free for academic use; excellent rendering
IFAO-Grec Unicode Polytonic plus papyrological symbols Free; strong for documentary texts
Noto Serif / Sans Good polytonic coverage Free; consistent cross-platform rendering

Install at least two. When a character fails to render, the diagnostic step is to view the file in a different font: if the second font shows the character, your data is fine and the first font simply lacked the glyph. If every font shows a box, the code point may genuinely be wrong — at which point you inspect code points as in the previous section.

For your XML editor and terminal, set a polytonic-capable monospace or serif face explicitly rather than accepting the default. A default font that silently fails on rare combinations will cost you an afternoon in Week 6, when you are working with exactly those combinations.

Takeaway: A missing glyph is a font problem, not a data problem; diagnose by changing fonts before changing files.

questiontext.text:
Keyboard Layouts and Input Methods

You will type a good deal of polytonic Greek this term, and the input method you choose determines both your speed and — critically — the normalization form of what you produce.

Method Platform Approach Typical output form
Greek Polytonic layout Windows, macOS, Linux System layout with dead keys for diacritics NFC on Windows; often NFD on macOS
Keyman (Galaxie / classical layouts) Cross-platform Installable layout with mnemonic input Configurable; usually NFC
Unicode hex input All Type the code point directly Exactly what you type
Copy from a digital corpus All Reuse existing text Whatever the source used — verify

The system polytonic layouts use dead keys: a key that produces no character itself but modifies the next keystroke. Typing the smooth-breathing dead key followed by alpha produces ἀ. Combinations chain, so breathing, accent, and iota subscript can be entered in sequence. The layouts repay a few hours of practice early in the term, and this weekend is the right time.

The last row of the table is the one to be careful about. Text copied from a digital corpus, a PDF, or a website arrives in whatever form that source used, which is frequently not NFC and occasionally not consistent within a single document. Always normalize after pasting, and never assume that text which looks right is encoded right.

Whatever method you adopt, verify its output once, deliberately: type a multi-diacritic character such as ᾧ, dump its code points, and learn what your own setup produces. Knowing your own tooling's default saves diagnosis later.

Takeaway: Verify what normalization form your own keyboard produces, and always normalize text pasted from external sources.

name.text: 18 Content: Oxygen XML Editor

questiontext.text:
Oxygen XML Editor

Oxygen is the standard professional environment for TEI work and is available to you through the university. Its advantage over a general text editor is that it understands the schema your document declares.

The features that matter for this course:

  • Schema-aware completion. With the TEI or EpiDoc schema associated, Oxygen offers only elements valid at the cursor position, which prevents a large class of encoding errors as you type (TEI Consortium, 2026; EpiDoc Guidelines, 2026).
  • Continuous validation. Errors are flagged as you work rather than at commit time, with the specific rule violated.
  • Author mode. A visual editing view driven by a stylesheet, useful when the raw markup becomes dense enough to obscure the text.
  • XPath evaluation. Query your own document interactively — indispensable from Week 8, when the apparatus makes documents large.
  • Built-in XSLT and transformation scenarios. Preview output without a separate toolchain.

Two configuration steps to take before Week 2. First, associate the TEI P5 schema with your documents so validation is live from the outset. Second, set the editor font to a polytonic-capable face from the previous section, and set the file encoding explicitly to UTF-8.

Oxygen also has Git integration adequate for staging and committing. It is perfectly acceptable to use it — with the caveat from Lesson 1.1 that graphical Git tools do not expose hooks, trailers, or pickaxe searches, so you will need the command line for those.

Takeaway: Oxygen's value is schema-aware validation as you type, catching encoding errors before they enter the repository.

name.text: 21 Content: Case Study: Structure-Aware OCR of Greek Critical Editions

questiontext.text:
Case Study: Structure-Aware OCR of Greek Critical Editions

A recent study illustrates why the encoding discipline in this lesson must precede any use of automation, and it is worth examining in detail because you will replicate a small version of it in Week 4.

Angleraud et al. (2026) address the digitization of printed Greek critical editions — a genuinely hard problem because the printed page is polycentric. A single page carries the primary text, a dense multi-layered apparatus at the foot, marginal line numbers, and canonical reference milestones such as Stephanus pagination embedded in the margins. Conventional OCR reads the page as a single column of text and interleaves these registers into an unusable transcript.

The researchers fine-tuned vision-language models — Qwen3-VL and DeepSeek-OCR-2 — on a synthetic corpus of 185,000 page images generated from TEI/XML sources with controlled typographic variation. The models were trained to emit structured output that explicitly separates the registers, marking milestones with <ref> and marginalia with <note> rather than flattening them into the text (Angleraud et al., 2026).

The results are worth reading carefully in both directions. The fine-tuned Qwen3-VL-8B model achieved a median character error rate of 1.0% — excellent by any standard, and better than most students achieve transcribing by hand. But the same study documents "catastrophic page-level failures," in which the model's output drifts entirely from the image and it generates fluent, grammatical, entirely fabricated Greek. The models also struggled systematically with symbolic ambiguity, particularly failing to distinguish alphabetic Greek numerals from ordinary lexical tokens (Angleraud et al., 2026).

That combination — excellent median accuracy with occasional total fabrication — is the defining risk profile of machine transcription, and it is why this course records provenance in commit trailers and measures error rates against your own ground truth. A model wrong 1% of the time uniformly could be trusted and spot- checked. A model that is 99% correct and occasionally invents a page cannot.

Takeaway: Machine transcription can achieve a 1.0% median error rate while occasionally fabricating entire pages, which is why provenance and ground truth are non-negotiable.

name.text: 22 Content: What the OCR Case Study Implies for Your Workflow

questiontext.text:
What the OCR Case Study Implies for Your Workflow

Draw out the consequences, because they shape how the rest of the term is structured.

If failures were uniformly distributed, sampling would be a valid quality control: check 10% of the output, estimate the error rate, and correct proportionally. Catastrophic page-level failure defeats sampling entirely, because the failures are concentrated and a sample may contain none of them while the document contains several (Angleraud et al., 2026).

If failures were visible, they would be self-correcting: fluent output that is obviously wrong gets caught. But a hallucinated page of Greek is grammatical and plausible. It reads as competent Greek because the model is very good at producing competent Greek — which is the source of the problem, not a mitigation of it. The only detection method is comparison against the image.

Failure profile Effective control Why
Uniform low-rate errors Sampling and spot-check Sample is representative of the whole
Concentrated catastrophic failure Full comparison against source Sample may miss the affected region entirely
Fluent fabrication Comparison against the image, not the text Output is internally plausible and self-consistent
Symbolic ambiguity (numerals) Targeted review of known-hard categories Failure is systematic and therefore predictable

Three practices follow, and each has a place later in the course. Every page of machine output is checked against the facsimile, not sampled. Machine output is committed separately from your corrections, so that the raw state remains recoverable and the error rate remains measurable. And known-hard categories — numerals, abbreviations, marginalia — receive targeted review rather than being trusted at the general rate.

Takeaway: Concentrated, fluent failures defeat sampling, so machine output must be compared page by page against the image.

name.text: 23 Content: Machine Learning and Philological Judgement

questiontext.text:
Machine Learning and Philological Judgement

The OCR case study concerns transcription. A second body of work concerns something more ambitious — machine assistance in editorial judgement — and it frames a question this course returns to repeatedly.

Cowen-Breen et al. (2023) describe Logion, a BERT-based model trained on premodern Greek, applied to the detection of scribal errors and the suggestion of emendations. The model learns the statistical regularities of Greek as attested in a large corpus, and can therefore identify passages that are anomalous with respect to those regularities — which is, in a limited but real sense, what a philologist does when a reading strikes them as wrong.

The limitation is precise and worth stating carefully. The model identifies statistical anomaly, not textual error. A passage may be unusual because a scribe erred, or because the author wrote something unusual — and authors of literary interest are, notoriously, the ones who write unusual things. The model cannot make that distinction, because the distinction requires knowing what the author was doing, which is not in the training data (Cowen-Breen et al., 2023).

This maps directly onto the Friday step of every week from Week 4 onward. The machine's proposal is evidence — genuinely useful evidence, of a kind that would take a human a long time to assemble. It is not a conclusion. Your task on those Fridays is to adjudicate the proposal against the manuscript and against your knowledge of the text, and to record in the commit body why you accepted or rejected it.

The pedagogical value of such tools may lie less in their proposals than in the articulation they force. Explaining why a statistically anomalous reading is nevertheless correct requires stating your reasoning explicitly — which is exactly the reasoning that Giarratano's print editions failed to preserve.

Takeaway: Language models detect statistical anomaly, not textual error, so their proposals are evidence for your judgement rather than substitutes for it.

name.text: 24 Content: Codicological Description and the Vocabulary of the Object

questiontext.text:
Codicological Description and the Vocabulary of the Object

Before selecting a passage, you need enough descriptive vocabulary to say what you are looking at. Comparative Oriental Manuscript Studies provides the standard framework for describing manuscripts as physical objects, and its terminology is what Week 2's cataloguing assignment will require (Bausi et al., 2015).

Term Refers to Why it matters for selection
Folio A leaf; recto is the front, verso the back Passage locations are cited as f. 42r, f. 42v
Quire / gathering A bundle of folded leaves forming a unit Quire boundaries often coincide with damage or loss
Ruling Lines guiding the script Affects legibility and line segmentation for HTR
Hand The writing of one scribe A change of hand mid-passage complicates model training
Lacuna A physical gap where text is lost Requires editorial restoration; adds difficulty
Palimpsest A reused leaf with erased underwriting Requires multispectral imaging; usually too hard for this term
Marginalia Notes added in the margins Must be encoded distinctly from the main text
Colophon A scribal note, often with date and place Valuable metadata for the Week 2 TEI header

Bausi et al. (2015) emphasize that codicological description is not preliminary to textual work but part of it: the physical structure of the book carries evidence about how the text was transmitted, and an edition that ignores the object is missing data.

For your purposes this week, this vocabulary is the checklist you take to the selection decision. You should be able to state, of the passage you choose, how many folios it spans, whether it is written in one hand, whether it contains lacunae or marginalia, and whether a colophon is present anywhere in the manuscript.

Takeaway: You need codicological vocabulary to describe what you have chosen, and the physical structure of the book is evidence, not context.

name.text: 25 Content: Choosing Your Passage: The Criteria That Matter

questiontext.text:
Choosing Your Passage: The Criteria That Matter

The selection due today governs the entire term. Every assignment from Week 2 to Week 13 operates on this passage, and a poor choice cannot be corrected in November. Weigh the following.

Criterion Target Why
Length 20–40 lines Enough for meaningful collation; small enough to encode fully
Legibility Clear, consistent hand HTR training in Week 4 requires readable baselines
Witnesses At least 2, ideally 3 Week 7 collation requires more than one witness
Image availability Open-licensed, high resolution Week 3 IIIF work requires images you may use
Textual interest Known variants or cruxes Weeks 8 and 12 need something to discuss
Prior editions At least one available Provides a comparison for your editorial decisions
Script Not a difficult minuscule or palimpsest Manageable within a thirteen-week term

The witness requirement is the one students most often underestimate. A passage surviving in a single manuscript makes Week 7's collation exercise impossible in any real sense — you cannot align witnesses you do not have, and substituting printed editions is a poor approximation of the exercise. Confirm that at least two witnesses are digitized and accessible before committing to a passage.

Image licensing is the second common failure. Many manuscript images are online but under restrictive terms; a IIIF manifest you cannot legally build or share undermines Week 3 and the final publication in Week 13. Prefer institutions with explicit open licensing — the Vatican Library, the British Library, the Bibliothèque nationale, e-codices, and similar repositories that publish IIIF endpoints openly.

Resist the temptation toward difficulty. A famously contested passage in a notoriously difficult hand is a compelling choice in September and an unfinishable one in November. Textual interest matters, but tractability matters more, and a clean passage encoded completely is worth more than an ambitious one abandoned in Week 9.

Takeaway: Confirm at least two accessible witnesses and open image licensing before committing; those two constraints eliminate most unworkable choices.

name.text: 26 Content: Verifying Your Choice Before Committing to It

questiontext.text:
Verifying Your Choice Before Committing to It

Do not select from a catalogue description alone. Run the following checks, all of which are quick and any of which can disqualify a passage.

  • Open the images. Confirm the resolution is sufficient to read individual letters when zoomed, not merely to identify the page.
  • Locate the IIIF manifest. Most major repositories expose a manifest URL; find it now, because Week 3 depends on it and its absence is a serious obstacle.
  • Check the licence explicitly. Find the stated terms, not an assumption. Note the required attribution formula.
  • Identify the second witness. Confirm it is digitized, accessible, and covers the same passage — not merely the same work.
  • Read ten lines. Actually attempt to read them. A hand that looks clear at page scale can be much harder at line scale.
  • Find one prior edition. Confirm a published text exists for comparison.
  • Check for a change of hand. Scan the passage boundaries for a shift in script.

If a passage fails on witnesses or on licensing, discard it and choose again — those two are not recoverable later. Failing on textual interest is survivable; failing on legibility is survivable if the passage is short. Failing on image resolution is not, because everything downstream depends on being able to read the source.

Bring the results of these checks to Week 2. The cataloguing assignment, due Friday September 18, will ask you to produce a TEI header describing this manuscript, and much of what the header needs — repository, shelfmark, date, material, extent, hand — is what you are gathering now (Bausi et al., 2015; TEI Consortium, 2026).

Takeaway: Verify images, manifest, licence, and second witness before committing to a passage; the first four checks are the ones that cannot be fixed later.

name.text: 27 Content: Recording the Choice in the Repository

questiontext.text:
Recording the Choice in the Repository

The selection is ungraded but not informal. Record it in your repository, as your first substantive commit, in a form that a reviewer can evaluate.

Your README.md should state:

  • The work, author, and passage reference (book, chapter, line, or folio range).
  • The primary manuscript: repository, shelfmark, date, and folio range.
  • The second and any further witnesses, with the same identifying detail.
  • The image source, IIIF manifest URL, and licence terms.
  • At least one prior edition, cited.
  • Two or three sentences on why you chose this passage.

The last item is the one that matters intellectually. Stating your reasons now produces a record you can evaluate later — in Week 10's consolidation session you will reread it and see whether the passage delivered what you expected, and in Week 13's publication you will have the beginning of an editorial introduction already written.

Commit it with a message that follows the conventions from Lesson 1.1:

docs(readme): select MS Vat. gr. 1209 ff. 42r-43v as edition passage

Chosen for a clear tenth-century minuscule hand, two further digitized
witnesses (BnF gr. 2934, BL Add. 17210), and open IIIF access via the
Vatican Library. Passage covers 34 lines with two known variants
discussed in the Wachtel edition, giving material for the Week 8
apparatus.

Note what that body does: it states the choice, gives the reasons against the selection criteria, and records the evidence that the criteria were met. Three months from now it is the only surviving record of why you are working on this text.

Takeaway: Record the passage and your reasons for choosing it as a committed document; it becomes the seed of your editorial introduction.

name.text: 28 Content: How the Encoding Foundation Carries Through the Term

questiontext.text:
How the Encoding Foundation Carries Through the Term

It is worth seeing where each element of this lesson reappears, because the material can feel like unmotivated preliminaries until it becomes load-bearing.

Established here Becomes essential in Consequence of neglect
NFC normalization Week 5 error rates Error rate inflated by encoding mismatch, not transcription error
Pre-commit hook Every week Unnormalized text accumulates and must be fixed retroactively
Code point inspection Weeks 5–7 Encoding faults misdiagnosed as transcription or collation faults
Polytonic font Weeks 4–6 Correct data mistaken for corruption; correct files "repaired"
Diacritic vocabulary Week 6 normalization Cannot state what is being normalized or justify the decision
Adscript / subscript distinction Week 6 Silent normalization of an editorial convention
Codicological vocabulary Week 2 TEI header Header incomplete; cataloguing assignment weakened
Passage with 2+ witnesses Week 7 collation Collation exercise cannot be performed as designed
Open image licence Weeks 3 and 13 IIIF manifest unbuildable; edition unpublishable

The pattern is that encoding problems do not present as encoding problems. They present as inexplicable error rates, spurious collation variants, mysterious diff noise, and files that look corrupted but are not. Every one of those symptoms sends students hunting in the wrong place, and the hours lost are hours not spent on the text.

This is why the course front-loads the infrastructure. Boschetti (2010) makes the same argument about corpus preparation: normalization is prerequisite to analysis, and analysis performed on unnormalized data yields results that are wrong without appearing wrong.

Takeaway: Encoding faults present as inexplicable error rates and phantom variants, which is why they must be eliminated before the analysis that would otherwise be blamed.

name.text: 30 Content: Synthesis: Infrastructure as Editorial Method

questiontext.text:
Synthesis: Infrastructure as Editorial Method

The two meetings of this week have covered version control and character encoding, which look like technical preliminaries to the real work of the course. They are not preliminaries. They are the conditions that make the real work possible, and the argument connecting them is worth stating explicitly.

An edition makes claims: this manuscript reads thus, this variant is to be preferred, this reading is corrupt. A scholarly edition additionally makes those claims inspectable — a reader can see what the evidence was and how the editor reasoned from it. Huskey (2024) frames this as reproducibility and explainability, and identifies version control as the mechanism that delivers both for a digital edition.

Character encoding is the same argument one level down. Before a claim about a reading can be inspected, the reading must be represented unambiguously. Text that is sometimes NFC and sometimes NFD does not make one claim; it makes a claim that varies by platform and by tool. Normalization is what makes the object of the claim stable enough to be argued about (Unicode Consortium, 2025).

Both, finally, are about the same thing: making your work checkable. The commit history lets a reader check your reasoning. Consistent encoding lets a machine check your text. The three-step cycle that begins in Week 2 — manual, then deterministic, then AI-assisted — is an extended exercise in checking, and it depends entirely on the two foundations laid this week.

Due today, Friday September 4. Your manuscript passage, selected against the criteria in section 25, verified by the checks in section 26, and recorded in a committed README.md. The selection is ungraded. Every graded assignment for the next twelve weeks builds on it.

Next week. Topic 2 begins the three-step cycle: Tuesday you hand-write a TEI header in a plain text editor, Wednesday you validate it against the schema in Oxygen and build RDF triples, and Friday you compare AI-generated metadata against the header you wrote yourself.

Takeaway: Version control makes your reasoning checkable and normalization makes your text checkable; the whole course is an exercise in checking, and this week built its preconditions.
